newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SOUTH AFRICA TO INTRODUCE AUTOMATED CARGO RELEASE.
newsitem.headline: SOUTH AFRICA TO INTRODUCE AUTOMATED CARGO RELEASE.

text.p: South African customs and excise will next month become one of the first countries in the world to start introducing an automated cargo release system to prevent fraud and illegal imports, Finance Minister Trevor Manuel said on Wednesday.
Answering questions during a mini-debate in the National Assembly, Manuel said that the system would go into operation in Johannesburg next month.
"We are in the process of testing and implementing an automated system for the electronic transfer of cargo release messages to Portnet, Spoornet and to the licensed container depots," he said.
"Live implementation is scheduled for early next month in Johannesburg."
Customs and excise had identified forged release documents as a major problem in cracking down on illegal imports.
"Currently all customs work is being done manually. Over and above that, different ports of entry, be they by sea, rail or land have different manual systems," he said.
As a result, it was relatively easy for importers to forge release documents before the necessary inspections had been undertaken and duties paid.

The department had tried to get round the problem by using faxes and hand delivered letters but on the advice of French and British customs officials it had been decided to adopt an electronic data interchange.
"We have been working on this system fairly intensely over the past 12 months," he said.
This would mean that instead of hard copy manifests, releases would be transmitted electronically from the shippers and as goods were cleared they would be automatically marked off.
The government was also planning to limit the number of border posts that could be used to import and export goods to help tighten up controls.

Safety and Security Minister Sydney Mufamadi last week announced that the clearing of commercial traffic into and out of South Africa would be limited to only 19 of its 52 border posts, with international air cargo cleared at only eight of its 36 airports.
